in_text_mentions: An atlas on the clinical presentation and differential diagnosis of PKDL has been published [48]. In field studies, macular lesions, which can spread to involve most parts of the body, are most common. In hospital-based studies, often cases with a long duration of PKDL are reported with extensive papular, nodular, or mixed presentations; special forms include erythrodermic, warty, lupoid, and tumour-like forms (Figs 2–4).

findings.evidence: Caption: "Bone marrow aspirate showing intrahistiocytic LD bodies - APD 5+. Inset shows neutrophil with intracellular LD bodies (MGG stain, 1000x)."

panels.rationale: Human bone marrow aspirate cytology from a visceral leishmaniasis article showing Leishman-Donovan/amastigote bodies within histiocytes, with an inset of intracellular LD bodies in a neutrophil; this is a specific diagnostic manifestation of visceral leishmaniasis.
panels.attribution_text: Mangat et al. The Morphological Landscape of Bone Marrow Findings in Visceral Leishmaniasis.. Cureus 2026. doi:10.7759/cureus.104000. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Bone marrow aspirate showing intrahistiocytic LD bodies - APD 5+. Inset shows neutrophil with intracellular LD bodies (MGG stain, 1000x). LD: Leishman-Donovan; APD: average parasite density; MGG: May-Grünwald Giemsa
in_text_mentions: The intercellular LD bodies in oil immersion are shown in Figures 1, 2. Average parasite density (APD) of grade 2+ was seen in 16 cases (38.10%), 3+ in 13 cases (30.95%), 1+ in six cases (14.29%), 4+ in four cases (9.52%), and 5+ in three cases (7.14%). Histological examination of bone marrow biopsy revealed hypercellularity (n=34; 80.95%), myelofibrosis (n=6; 14.29%), granulomas (n=3; 7.14%), and single cases showed gelatinous transformation (2.38%). APD showed significant associations with splenomegaly (χ²=4.67; p=0.031), pancytopenia (χ²=5.57; p=0.018), and plasmacytosis (χ²=5.12; p=0.024)

findings.label: Leishman-Donovan bodies in aspirate
findings.evidence: Caption: "Phagocytosed Leishmania donovani bodies within macrophages in a bone marrow smear from Case A (Wright-Giemsa staining × 1,000)"; in-text: "a second bone marrow aspiration that revealed LD bodies (Figures 1 and 2)"

panels.rationale: Wright-Giemsa-stained bone marrow aspirate smear from a real patient (Case A) with confirmed visceral leishmaniasis, showing a macrophage engorged with intracellular Leishmania donovani amastigotes (Leishman-Donovan bodies) — the hallmark diagnostic finding of Kala-azar. Disease attribution is strongly supported by the caption, in-text mention, and disease-focused article title.

The American journal of tropical medicine and hygiene 2026. doi:10.4269/ajtmh.25-0530. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Phagocytosed Leishmania donovani bodies within macrophages in a bone marrow smear from Case A (Wright-Giemsa staining × 1,000).
in_text_mentions: agnostic confirmation varied among cases: Case A was confirmed after repeated history-taking revealed exposure to endemic regions, followed by a second bone marrow aspiration that revealed LD bodies (Figures 1 and 2). Cases B and C were diagnosed through subsequent bone marrow aspirations that directly revealed LD bodies. Case D was confirmed when mNGS of blood samples revealed Leishmania, prompting reexamination of bone marrow smears, which then revealed LD bodies (Supplemental Figures 1 and 2). The time from initial presentation to definitive diagnosis ranged from 17 days (Case A) to 7 month

in_text_mentions: Additionally, the histological images provided suffer from poor magnification and structural clarity, making the definitive identification of Leishman-Donovan (LD) bodies highly speculative. Standard Giemsa staining typically imparts a distinct purple hue to the kinetoplast and nucleus of amastigotes (see Figure 1 example provided here); this coloration is unconvincing in Figure 2 of the published report. For a definitive diagnosis of VL/PKDL, high-magnification confirmation or molecular corroboration via nucleic acid amplification tests should have been pursued.

panels.figure_caption: Leishmania amastigotes could be identified in the bone marrow trephine of all patients, in variable amounts. In Case 3, intertrabecular lacunae were hypercellular and numerous macrophages phagocyting significant numbers of amastigotes were evident and could be easily observed (A–D). In Cases 1 and 2, parasitic infection was more subtle with only a few amastigotes identifiable in rare macrophages ((E) and (F), respectively). In Case 1, cellularity was increased, while in Case 2, it was normal and hematopoietic progenitors of the three series displayed signs of abnormal maturation.
in_text_mentions: ection or infective diathesis. He owned a dog, who appeared to be healthy and tested negative for Leishmania. The patient never acquired SARS-CoV-2 infection and received two shots of the Comirnaty vaccine in March 2021. Since then, he experienced weight loss, fatigue, and night sweats. In June 2021, he underwent a bone marrow biopsy on the suspicion of a primary hemopathy, which produced negative results. Due to the persistence of the same symptoms, he repeated the procedure in October 2021, which demonstrated the presence of Leishmania amastigotes in the patient’s bone marrow (see Figure 2).
She was transferred to the infectious diseases ward and a bone marrow biopsy revealed amastigotes (see Figure 2). qPCR on peripheral blood detected L. infantum.

Since August 2021, he suffered from night sweats, fatigue, and intermittent fever. He presented with pancytopenia, hypergammaglobulinemia (two monoclonal gammopathies), and moderate splenomegaly. Upon the suspicion of a primary hemopathy, he was subjected to a bone marrow biopsy with the finding of numerous amastigotes (see Figure 2).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: May–Grünwald–Giemsa-stained bone marrow aspirate smear from a human patient (case 1) of imported visceral leishmaniasis, showing hypercellular marrow with Leishmania amastigotes within macrophages; classic diagnostic cytology image. B: Hypercellular bone marrow aspirate smear packed with parasitized macrophages containing Leishmania amastigotes; real human patient cytology confirming visceral leishmaniasis. C: Lower-power view of the marrow smear showing macrophages engorged with intracellular amastigotes, consistent with visceral leishmaniasis in a human patient. D: Marrow smear showing numerous free extracellular Leishmania amastigotes as stated in the caption for panel D; extracellular predominance is a less commonly emphasized presentation, hence variant. The extracellular pattern is not in the allowed vocabulary, so it is proposed.

in_text_mentions: to rule out hematolymphoid malignancy was done. Abdominal CT scan and USG showed splenomegaly without focal mass, measuring up to 19.5 cm. Bone marrow aspiration with flow cytometry, and peripheral blood with flow cytometry showed no significant findings. He then underwent a splenic core biopsy. The biopsy showed splenic tissue with granulomatous chronic inflammation with numerous organisms (Figure 2). in_text_mentions: In the presence of underlying immune deficiency, fever, and loss of appetite, Mantoux and sputum acid-fast bacillus (AFB) were performed, which resulted in negative. Therefore, bone marrow was performed, which showed inclusions in macrophages suggestive of Leishmania donovani bodies (Figure 2). Thus, the diagnosis of reactivation of leishmaniasis was made.

panels.rationale: Single-panel abdominal ultrasound from a confirmed visceral leishmaniasis case (rK39 Kalazar Detect positive, classic kala-azar presentation) showing marked splenomegaly of 14.35 cm with homogeneous echotexture and no focal mass. Massive splenomegaly is a textbook manifestation of visceral leishmaniasis, and the caption and in-text context directly attribute this finding to the disease. Measurement calipers and the on-image distance readout (1 Dist 14.35 cm) are present. No age or ethnicity is stated in the caption or provided in-text mentions.

in_text_mentions: y, tuberculosis was considered, as it often presents with extrapulmonary involvement in Borama [5]. Tests for malaria, tuberculosis (Mantoux), enteric fever (Widal), and H. pylori were negative. Due to the lack of specialized personnel and equipment for splenic/bone marrow aspiration, definitive parasitological microscopy was not performed. An rK39 antigen‐based rapid diagnostic test (Kalazar Detect) was positive (Figure 1). Abdominal ultrasonography confirmed hepatomegaly (liver span 18.87 cm; Figure 2) and marked splenomegaly (spleen length 14.35 cm; Figure 3) with a homogeneous echotexture.

panels.rationale: Single-panel Giemsa-stained splenic aspirate microscopy image from a confirmed visceral leishmaniasis case (article title and in-text diagnosis). The field shows numerous Leishmania donovani amastigotes (LD bodies), both extracellular and within a large central macrophage, matching the caption and the reported 4+ parasite grade (251 LD bodies/100 OIF). This is the classic diagnostic histologic presentation of visceral leishmaniasis; no diagrams, controls, or other diseases are present.

in_text_mentions: aldehyde test was performed which was strongly positive. In view of the strong clinical suspicion of VL and the positive aldehyde test, splenic aspiration was done. Aspirates showed both intracellular as well as extracellular amastigote forms of LD bodies, thus confirming VL (Fig. 1). A combination therapy was started with pulse liposomal amphotericin B (10 mg/kg body weight) i.e. 250 mg as a single dose therapy followed by tablet miltefosine 50mg O.D. for one week. panels.rationale: Single-panel bone marrow aspiration cytology (Giemsa-type stain) from a human patient with pancytopenia, diagnosed as visceral leishmaniasis. The white arrow marks a macrophage whose cytoplasm is engorged with Leishmania amastigotes (Leishman-Donovan bodies), the textbook diagnostic finding of kala-azar. Disease attribution is directly supported by the caption, the in-text description, and the disease-focused article title; no other disease, control, or third-party material is involved.

in_text_mentions: ts ( Table 1). The results of typical serological tests were negative. Bone marrow aspiration was evaluated because of pancytopenia in which no blast cell was seen. Then, due to observation of amastigotes of Leishmania parasite (Leishman-Donovan bodies) within bone marrow macrophages, and the positive DAT result (>1:3200), visceral leishmaniasis was diagnosed ( Figure 2). Therefore, Amphotericin-B treatment was initiated with dose of 1 mg/kg for 21 days. After four days, the patient’s fever disappeared, her general condition improved and blood cell number increased at the next month follow-up.

in_text_mentions: Also, the liver was slightly larger than the normal size. Due to the fever and enlarged spleen, bone marrow aspiration and biopsy were performed. The results of bone marrow pathology revealed the typical appearance of leishmania amastigotes, each with a nucleus and a kinetoplast within histiocytes (Figure 2). Moreover, the results of PCR confirmed Leishmania infantum resulting in the visceral form of leishmaniasis (Figure 3). Upon diagnosis, amphotericin B was injected at 1 mg/kg for about one month. Then, afterward, the patient's symptoms gradually subsided and her general condition improved.

this region, the physician suspected to visceral leishmaniasis and bone marrow puncture performed. The disease was diagnosed based on observing the amastigote shape of parasite in bone marrow aspiration and biopsy (Figure 2) and confirmed with PCR (Figure 3). panels.rationale: Bone marrow aspirate cytology image with an arrow pointing to intracellular amastigotes (Leishman-Donovan bodies) within macrophages; caption and in-text explicitly confirm this established the diagnosis of visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar). The large central macrophage engorged with numerous amastigotes plus scattered extracellular amastigotes is the textbook diagnostic presentation. No ethnicity or age stated in caption or in-text.

panels.figure_caption: Microscopic analysis of bone marrow aspirate showing intracellular amastigotes within macrophages (black arrow).
in_text_mentions: Given the history and the presenting complaints, the patient was tested to rule out malaria, typhoid, infectious mononucleosis, and tuberculosis. The negative results of the differential diagnoses and pancytopenia prompted a bone marrow biopsy. Microscopic analysis of the bone marrow aspirate revealed several Leishman-Donovan (LD) bodies. Numerous intracellular and extracellular amastigotes were seen in the aspirate, thus confirming the diagnosis of visceral leishmaniasis or kala-azar. The bone marrow findings are shown below (Figure 1).

panels.rationale: Single-panel gross autopsy photograph of the opened abdominal cavity of the reported visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) patient, showing a massively enlarged dark-purple spleen together with an enlarged liver. The caption states 'massive splenomegaly and hepatomegaly,' and the in-text mentions describe 'massive organ manifestations of VL' found at autopsy in this confirmed visceral leishmaniasis case, so disease attribution is direct. Massive splenomegaly is the classic textbook manifestation of kala-azar. Hepatomegaly is equally visible and captioned but has no vocabulary key, so it is recorded as a proposed finding. No arrows, labels or scale annotations are present. Neither the caption nor the in-text mentions state the patient's age or ethnicity, so both are null/unknown.

panels.rationale: Real-patient abdominal ultrasound from a confirmed visceral leishmaniasis case (bone marrow aspirate with Leishmania amastigotes) showing homogeneous splenomegaly measuring 18 cm (180.4 mm on-image caliper measurement). Splenomegaly is a classic manifestation of visceral leishmaniasis, and the article title plus in-text context directly attribute this image to the VL case.

in_text_mentions: In hospital, pancytopenia was confirmed and further investigation initiated. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated mild hepatomegaly (16.5 cm, Figure 1) and homogeneous splenomegaly (18 cm, Figure 2). Bone marrow aspirate revealed hypocellularity with the presence of Leishmania amastigotes, identified by the clinical pathology laboratory, confirming the diagnosis of visceral leishmaniasis (Figures 3, 4). Immunophenotyping and karyotype (46,XY) showed no pathological abnormalities.

panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph of a real patient (50-year-old man, consented) showing hypopigmented papules and plaques on the face, peri-orally and on the cheeks, in a patient with documented prior visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) treated 15 months earlier with confirmed Leishmania donovani DNA. This is the classic facial presentation of post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis, a recognized manifestation of visceral leishmaniasis, matching the configured target disease. Skin tone judged directly from the adequately lit facial skin as dark; no ethnicity stated; no image annotations present. [raw subtype: post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL)]

in_text_mentions: A 50-year-old man from Mymensingh district, Bangladesh, presented with a 3-month history of non-pruritic, painless hypopigmented papules, and plaques, beginning on the face and subsequently spreading to the forearms, torso, and legs (Figures 1–4) Fifteen months before the onset of skin lesions, the patient had visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar), successfully treated with 30 intramuscular injections of sodium stibogluconate (SSG). Polymerase chain reaction showed Leishmania donovani DNA in a buffy coat specimen.

panels.figure_caption: A 55-year-old man presented with a fever for 1 month. Routine diagnostic testing for fever of unknown origin (FUO) did not lead to the diagnosis of etiology. The patient was referred to the Department of Nuclear Medicine for an 18F-FDG PET/CT scan (axial CT, enhanced CT, PET, fusion, and maximum intensity projection (MIP)). Axial non-contrast CT (A) only revealed splenomegaly. However, PET (E) and fusion (F) images showed diffuse FDG uptake in the enlarged spleen with a maximum standardized uptake value (SUV max) of 6.6. The MIP image (G) displayed increased FDG uptake in the enlarged spleen, accompanied by multiple low-density nodules with delayed enhancement on abdominal enhanced CT (B–D), which were similar to those found in lymphoma. Based on pathological examination, a diagnosis of visceral leishmaniasis (VL) was made following splenectomy. The patient received treatment with amphotericin B and was discharged from hospital without fever.

panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph of both forearms showing hypopigmented papules and plaques in a 50-year-old man with a prior episode of treated visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar), confirming post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL), a manifestation of visceral leishmaniasis. Prior caption triage kept it as a real human-patient clinical photo. The dark skin is judged from the visibly lit forearms; no ethnicity is stated verbatim, so it is null. [raw subtype: post-kala-azar_dermal_leishmaniasis_PKDL]
panels.attribution_text: Islam et al. Post-Kala-Azar dermal leishmaniasis in Mymensingh, Bangladesh.. The American journal of tropical medicine and hygiene 2011. doi:10.4269/ajtmh.2011.11-0128. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 4.
panels.figure_caption: The patient has hypopigmented papules and plaques on both forearms. The absence of sensorineural changes helps to distinguish post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL) from leprosy, which commonly presents with hypopigmented macules or patches associated with hypoesthesia or anesthesia, and neural thickening.
in_text_mentions: A 50-year-old man from Mymensingh district, Bangladesh, presented with a 3-month history of non-pruritic, painless hypopigmented papules, and plaques, beginning on the face and subsequently spreading to the forearms, torso, and legs (Figures 1–4) Fifteen months before the onset of skin lesions, the patient had visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar), successfully treated with 30 intramuscular injections of sodium stibogluconate (SSG). Polymerase chain reaction showed Leishmania donovani DNA in a buffy coat specimen.

in_text_mentions: The antinuclear antibodies screen was negative. Immunoglobulin G (IgG) was markedly elevated at 5.3 g/dL; however, serum protein electrophoresis did not reveal an M spike. A peripheral smear showed microcytic, hypochromic red blood cells with mild anisopoikilocytosis and leukocytosis with a left shift. Metamyelocytes were present, and there were no giant platelets or platelet aggregates. A CT abdomen and pelvis without IV contrast revealed hepatomegaly, splenomegaly with heterogeneous density, and a left renal hypodensity (Figure 1).

findings.label: Hypopigmented macules in post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis
findings.evidence: Caption: 'Infiltrated hypopigmented plaques on the nape of the neck and upper back'; in-text: 'hypopigmented patches on the face, ears, neck, and trunk (Figure 1)'

panels.rationale: Clear clinical photograph of a real human patient showing infiltrated hypopigmented plaques on the nape of the neck and upper back. Although the patient was initially diagnosed with leprosy in reaction, the article title ('Postkala-Azar Dermal and Visceral Leishmaniasis in a Patient from Bangladesh') establishes that these hypopigmented lesions represent post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL), a well-recognized cutaneous manifestation of visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar). The hypopigmented macules/patches match the vocabulary finding visceral_leishmaniasis_pkdl_hypopigmented_macules and constitute a classic PKDL presentation. The patient is stated to be a 35-year-old Bangladeshi man (adult); skin tone is judged directly from the visible, adequately lit skin as medium (Fitzpatrick III-IV). The image is clear and substantial, with no third-party copyright indication; the small corner logo is a publisher watermark, not a clinical annotation. [raw subtype: post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL)]
panels.attribution_text: Kwan et al. Postkala-Azar Dermal and Visceral Leishmaniasis in a Patient from Bangladesh.. The American journal of tropical medicine and hygiene 2026. doi:10.4269/ajtmh.26-0159. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Infiltrated hypopigmented plaques on the nape of the neck and upper back.
in_text_mentions: A 35-year-old Bangladeshi man presented in April 2024 with a 1-year history of infiltrated plaques and hypopigmented patches on the face, ears, neck, and trunk (Figure 1). Slit-skin smears (SSSs) from both earlobes and the right elbow were positive for acid-fast bacilli. Chest histology showed superficial perivascular chronic inflammation without granulomas and was negative for acid-fast bacilli on Ziehl–Neelsen and Fite stains. He was diagnosed with leprosy in reaction and treated with WHO multidrug therapy (dapsone, rifampicin, and clofazimine) and prednisolone. His lesions initially resolve

in_text_mentions: bone marrow sample originating from the same sample used for mNGS was collected and placed under microscopic examination. Result revealed reticular cells, hemophagocytosis and Leishmania amastigotes ( Figures 3A–D ), indicating a potential Leishmania infection. Consistent with these results, the mNGS results of BM sample showed that Leishmania-positive sequences were detected at a high relative abundance of 99.52% ( Table 3 , Figure 4 ). The patient had no abnormal medical or family history, but had previously resided in a mountainous region where sporadic leishmaniasis had previously occurred

in_text_mentions: A bone marrow biopsy was performed in view his pancytopenia and it showed amastigotes (see figure 1). The Leishmania PCR test detected DNA from the Leishmania donovani complex. Furthermore, the patient’s Leishmania serology was strongly positive at a titre equal to or greater than 1 in 102 400 (a titre of 1 in 1600 or above is considered positive). His peripheral blood PCR for Leishmania was negative.

VL is diagnosed through identifying amastigotes in tissue (figure 1) or flagellated promastigotes in culture. Splenic aspirates are the gold standard with a sensitivity of >95%. In experienced hands, splenic aspiration is safe provided the patient has a normal prothrombin time and a platelet count greater than 40×109/L. Bone marrow aspiration is more commonly used and detects 85% of cases.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Axial abdominal CT of a human patient with fever, weight loss and splenomegaly in a case report of visceral leishmaniasis; the caption and in-text describe significant splenomegaly with inhomogeneous splenic parenchyma, a classic imaging manifestation of visceral leishmaniasis. B: Abdominal ultrasound of the same human patient showing an enlarged spleen with diffusely inhomogeneous parenchyma; the article is a case report of visceral leishmaniasis with splenomegaly confirmed on imaging, so the panel directly supports a classic visceral leishmaniasis manifestation.

in_text_mentions: ompt surgical consultation at the Clinical Center of Serbia, Belgrade, a clinic for abdominal surgery. Over the previous 3 months, the patient had experienced episodes of abdominal pain, malaise, fever, and repeated nose bleeding accompanied by weight loss of around 20 kg. The patient provided anamnestic information that during the last year he worked on a cruise ship on the Mediterranean route, including North African countries. On admission, no signs of hemorrhagic diathesis were observed. Abdomen ultrasonography and computed tomographic scanning revealed significant splenomegaly (Figure 2).

in_text_mentions: diffuse redness throughout the tracheobronchial tree. Inflammation was more prominent on the medial aspect of the bronchus intermedius extending into the middle lobe bronchus. Bronchial biopsies taken from this lesion revealed epithelial hyperplasia and several Leishmania amastigotes within histiocytes (Figures 2(a) and 2(b)). panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Real-patient abdominal ultrasound from a Kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis) case report; intercostal spleen thickness ~7.0 cm demonstrates marked splenomegaly, a hallmark visceral leishmaniasis manifestation, in a disease-focused article (mNGS-diagnosed Kala-Azar). B: Real-patient abdominal ultrasound showing hepatomegaly with parenchymal damage, a recognized visceral leishmaniasis manifestation, in the disease-focused Kala-Azar case; hepatomegaly is not in the allowed vocabulary so it is recorded as a proposed finding. C: Real-patient shear-wave elastography of the liver (hardness 12.3 kPa) in the same Kala-Azar patient, reflecting hepatic parenchymal involvement/fibrosis; fibrosis is a less specific, less common sequela of visceral leishmaniasis, so confidence is moderate and the finding is recorded as proposed rather than from the fixed vocabulary.

in_text_mentions: is with hyperplastic changes along with characteristic findings revealing histiocytes with phagocytosed red blood cells, WBC, and platelets, a characteristic microscopy finding reflecting HLH (Figure 1). Active hemophagocytosis was frequent, counting about 1-2 histiocytes with ingested blood cells per high-power field, and in some fields, the count was even more (Figure 2). Further evaluation of the bone marrow revealed numerous amastigote forms of Leishmania present intracellularly, particularly within macrophages, and extracellularly as well. No findings suggesting malignancies or any other

l, often known as kala-azar and the most severe form of the disease (VL); (2) cutaneous, the most common (CL); and (3) mucocutaneous. Visceral leishmaniasis is the most severe as it can become fatal if not treated and is characterized by persistent irregular fever and splenomegaly [18]. The etiologic diagnosis of HLH disease is challenging to make based on patient symptoms alone [19]. Bone marrow findings are informative in identifying amastigote forms of Leishmania seen within macrophages and extracellularly along with characteristic hemophagocytosis, as demonstrated in Figure 1 and Figure 3.

panels.rationale: Single-panel bone marrow aspirate microscopy image from a human patient with confirmed visceral leishmaniasis (K39 IgM positive, clinical response to pentavalent antimonials). Caption explicitly identifies Leishman-Donovan bodies outside macrophages and in-text describes Leishmania amastigotes within macrophages; the image shows a parasitized macrophage with multiple amastigote nuclei alongside extracellular LD bodies, the textbook diagnostic manifestation of visceral leishmaniasis. No third-party indication; prior triage keeps it.

panels.rationale: Single whole-body 18F-FDG PET (MIP) from the article 'Visceral Leishmaniasis Mimicking Aggressive Lymphoma'. It is a real patient radiology image (prior triage: keep, not third-party) showing hypermetabolic splenomegaly and hepatomegaly with diffuse osteomedullary hypermetabolism. Disease attribution to visceral_leishmaniasis is supported by the disease-focused article title plus the captioned splenomegaly/hepatomegaly in a VL patient, satisfying the panel-specific-evidence rule; splenomegaly is the hallmark VL manifestation. The FDG-PET pattern mimicking lymphoma is a less common/recognized presentation rather than the textbook ultrasound picture, so typicality is variant. No skin, nails, lips or oral mucosa are assessable on a PET MIP, so skin_tone is null; no ethnicity or age is stated. Hepatomegaly and diffuse osteomedullary hypermetabolism are clearly present but absent from the vocabulary, so they are listed as proposed findings.

panels.figure_caption: 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) PET/CT scan shows hypermetabolic splenomegaly and hepatomegaly. Small axillary lymphadenopathies appear reactive. Additionally, diffuse osteomedullary hypermetabolism is noted.
in_text_mentions: lic splenomegaly (SUVmax 14.7), homogeneous hepatic and diffuse bone marrow hypermetabolism, as well as sub-centimetric hypermetabolic right axillary lymph nodes, mildly hypermetabolic cervical and right subpectoral lymph nodes, and bilateral nonspecific tonsillar hypermetabolism (Figure 1). A bone marrow biopsy was performed and showed normal findings, while a liver biopsy revealed Kupffer cell hyperplasia and some evidence of phagocytosis without evidence of lymphoma. The absence of monoclonal lymphocytes was also confirmed by flow cytometry on both peripheral blood and bone marrow aspirate.

panels.rationale: Single high-power MGG-stained bone marrow aspirate from a visceral leishmaniasis article. The caption identifies hemophagocytosis and the in-text explicitly states intercellular LD bodies are shown in Figures 1 and 2, supporting VL attribution; the image shows a parasitized/engorged macrophage with hemophagocytosis. This is a real human-patient diagnostic smear with no annotations.
panels.attribution_text: Mangat et al. The Morphological Landscape of Bone Marrow Findings in Visceral Leishmaniasis.. Cureus 2026. doi:10.7759/cureus.104000. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Bone marrow aspirate showing hemophagocytosis (MGG stain, 1000x). MGG: May-Grünwald Giemsa
in_text_mentions: The intercellular LD bodies in oil immersion are shown in Figures 1, 2. Average parasite density (APD) of grade 2+ was seen in 16 cases (38.10%), 3+ in 13 cases (30.95%), 1+ in six cases (14.29%), 4+ in four cases (9.52%), and 5+ in three cases (7.14%). Histological examination of bone marrow biopsy revealed hypercellularity (n=34; 80.95%), myelofibrosis (n=6; 14.29%), granulomas (n=3; 7.14%), and single cases showed gelatinous transformation (2.38%). APD showed significant associations with splenomegaly (χ²=4.67; p=0.031), pancytopenia (χ²=5.57; p=0.018), and plasmacytosis (χ²=5.12; p=0.024)

in_text_mentions: led erythroid hyperplasia, with normoblastic erythropoiesis. The myeloid series was found to be active with moderate histiocytes and moderate dysplasia, and the plasma cell count was slightly increased. There was a prominent megakaryocytic series. There was an abundant amount of L. donovani bodies intracellularly within the macrophages and extracellularly (Figure 1). Based on the bone marrow examination results, the child was diagnosed as having VL (kala-azar) and immediately underwent treatment.

The caption explicitly attributes these lesions to post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis, a well-recognized sequela of visceral leishmaniasis, and the in-text description confirms the same. The article reports an autochthonous case of visceral leishmaniasis in Tanzania. The image is clear, adequately lit, and shows a real patient; the black bar over the eyes is anonymization, not an author annotation. Skin is assessable and dark (Fitzpatrick V-VI). No age or ethnicity is stated, so both are unknown. [raw subtype: post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis]

panels.body_site: face/nose, left wrist dorsum, right index finger
panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph of a real human patient showing infiltrated erythematous plaques on the nose, left wrist dorsum, and right index finger. The article and in-text mentions confirm post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (a recognized sequela of visceral leishmaniasis/kala-azar) in a 45-year-old HIV-positive man with a prior 6-month history of kala-azar and Leishman-Donovan bodies on slit skin smear. The facial plaques fit the classic PKDL presentation; extremity plaques are consistent with the same disease. Eyes are anonymized with a black bar. [raw subtype: post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL)]
panels.attribution_text: Shah et al. Post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis in HIV-positive patients: A study of two cases.. Indian journal of sexually transmitted diseases and AIDS 2010. doi:10.4103/0253-7184.69001. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Infiltrated plaques on nose, left dorsum of wrist and on index finger of right hand
in_text_mentions: A 45-year-old HIV-positive man presented with nodules and plaques on nasal area, dorsum of left wrist, right index finger, and back with cervical lymph adenopathy [Figure 1]. Patient had history of fever 6 months back when he was working in state of Bihar. Patient also complained of mild pyrexia off and on and weight loss. Routine blood and urine examination did not reveal any abnormalities. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay test for HIV was positive, and CD4 Count was 210/μL. Slit skin smear with giemsa stain revealed abundant intra- and extracellular leishman donovan bodies.

BM trephine biopsy showed cells with granules, suspect for intracellular parasite of the type of leishmania (Figure 2, A-B)

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: High-power (X400) HE-stained bone marrow trephine biopsy from a patient with confirmed visceral leishmaniasis (positive BM PCR) showing intracellular Leishmania amastigotes (Leishman-Donovan bodies) within marrow cells, marked by blue arrows; the classic diagnostic histologic finding of VL. B: Low-power (X100) HE-stained bone marrow biopsy overview from the same patient showing Leishmania parasites in the marrow; diagnosis of visceral leishmaniasis confirmed by positive PCR for leishmanias in the BM per in-text mention.
panels.attribution_text: Diamantidis et al. Hemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis as a Manifestation of Underlying Visceral Leishmaniasis.. Cureus 2020. doi:10.7759/cureus.11911. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Bone Marrow Biopsy A. Cells with granules, suspect for intracellular parasite of the type of leishmania (blue arrows). Hematoxylin and Eosin (HE) stain X 400; B. Overall imaging of the bone marrow showing leishmanias. Hematoxylin and Eosin (HE) stain X 100
in_text_mentions: Finally, 19 days after the initial admission of the patient, BM trephine biopsy showed cells with granules, suspect for intracellular parasite of the type of leishmania (Figure 2, A-B). A positive PCR for leishmanias in the BM further confirmed the diagnosis of VL. Even though there was strong suspicion for leishmaniasis from day five (BM aspiration), the final diagnosis was established on day 19 and etiological treatment was initiated on day 23.

panels.rationale: Single-panel clinical photograph of a patient's back showing multiple hypo- and hyperpigmented macular and maculopapular non-scaly lesions, with a yellow arrow highlighting one lesion. The article is a case report of para kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis, a cutaneous post/para-kala-azar manifestation of visceral leishmaniasis, and the in-text description matches the classic PKDL skin presentation. This is a real human-patient image with a specific clinical manifestation of the configured target disease. [raw subtype: para_kala_azar_dermal_leishmaniasis]

panels.figure_caption: multiple hypo and hyper pigmented macular and maculopapular non-scaly skin lesions present all over the body, mostly on the back and abdomen (yellow arrow)
in_text_mentions: Examination revealed multiple hypo and hyperpigmented macular and maculopapular non-scaly skin lesions present all over the body, mainly on the back of the chest and abdomen. Lesions were a few millimeters (0.3-0.7 mm) (those hypo-pigmented) to a few centimeters (1-3 cm) (those hyper-pigmented) in diameter (Fig 1), and sensation over the lesions was intact. Other vital parameters were normal. On abdominal examination, there was firm, non-tender hepato-splenomegaly (liver 4 cm from the right costal margin and spleen 6 cm from its long axis).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Whole-body 18F-FDG PET maximum-intensity projection from a real patient with PCR-confirmed Leishmania donovani visceral leishmaniasis (article title and in-text: bone marrow biopsy with intracellular microorganisms, PCR confirmation). The caption documents homogeneously increased FDG uptake in the bone marrow, and the in-text confirms tracer enhancement in central and peripheral bone marrow; bone marrow involvement is a specific manifestation of visceral leishmaniasis, so the disease attribution is strong. Diagnostic imaging of untreated disease, not a diagram, control, animal, or third-party image; kept. No vocabulary key covers bone marrow PET hypermetabolism, so the clearly visible finding is recorded as proposed findings. Skin tone, ethnicity, and age are not assessable/stated. B: Axial 18F-FDG PET/CT through the upper abdomen from the same confirmed visceral leishmaniasis case, showing an enlarged spleen with homogeneously increased...
panels.attribution_text: Schwetz et al. Visceral leishmaniasis in a patient with diabetes mellitus type 2 and discrete bicytopenia.. Clinical case reports 2018. doi:10.1002/ccr3.1259. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: (A) Homogeneously increased 18F‐FDG‐uptake in the bone marrow. (B) Homogeneously increased 18F‐FDG‐uptake in the spleen. PET/CT scan was performed using a dedicated 64‐slice body PET/CT scanner (Biograph mCT). A 6‐h fasting period is required before the intravenous injection of the activity of 356 MBq 18F‐FDG can be applied. Imaging was started with a low‐dose CT of the whole body 1 h after the injection. PET scans were performed in caudocranial direction with 2 min per bed position.
in_text_mentions: Positron emission tomography–computed tomography (see Fig. 1A and B) showed tracer enhancement in the central and peripheral bone marrow. Bone marrow biopsy revealed microorganisms within macrophages (Fig. 2). PCR from peripheral blood and bone marrow confirmed infection with Leishmania donovani. Therapy with liposomal amphotericin B was initiated, causing rapid cessation of fever and a significant drop in CRP levels within days. Blood count ameliorated rapidly, and transfusions were no longer required. After release from hospital, regular follow‐up visits at the outpatient clinic ensued. Unti

panels.rationale: Axial fused FDG-PET/CT from a case report titled 'Acute liver failure due to visceral leishmaniasis in Barcelona: a case report.' The caption documents diffuse high FDG uptake in the spleen (SUV max 13.26), liver, and bone marrow without lymph node involvement, and the image shows a markedly enlarged, intensely FDG-avid spleen consistent with massive splenomegaly in visceral leishmaniasis. The diffuse multi-organ FDG uptake pattern is not covered by the allowed vocabulary and is recorded as a proposed finding. No skin, ethnicity, or age information is stated.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: PAS-stained renal cortical tissue from patient 2, a PCR-confirmed Leishmania infantum case with type III MPGN described in a disease-focused article on visceral leishmaniasis with renal involvement. The panel shows cortical kidney inflammation, the renal manifestation of VL in this confirmed patient; attribution rests on the disease-focused title plus the captioned manifestation, but the inflammation itself is nonspecific, so confidence is moderate. B: Trichrome-stained renal biopsy showing clusters of free Leishmania parasites within a capillary lumen, directly visualizing the amastigote (Leishman-Donovan body) stage that is the diagnostic hallmark of visceral leishmaniasis; the patient was Leishmania infantum PCR-positive. C: Silver-stained glomerulus from the same confirmed visceral leishmaniasis patient showing prominent double-contour formations, a type III MPGN feature. The disease-focused article (VL with renal involvement)...

He also reported difficulty swallowing, odynophagia, and feeling a mass during swallowing, which progressively worsened. Two weeks before the presentation, he started to have gum bleeding, high-grade intermittent fever, loss of appetite, and unquantified significant weight loss.

On physical examination, his vital signs were stable. The soft palate and pharynx were diffusely swollen and erythematous (Figure 2B). There was bilateral submandibular lymphadenopathy (1 cm × 1 cm). There was an enlarged spleen (6 cm below the left costal margin) and liver (2 cm below the right costal margin). There were multiple small, macular, patchy hypopigmented lesions on the face (Figure 2A). The complete blood count and renal and liver function tests were in the normal range.
